section: Fundamental Rights - Article 12 (State), Article 13 and doctrines of eclipse, severability, waiver
subsections: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: Which doctrine states that a law is void only to the extent of its inconsistency with Fundamental Rights, while the separable valid portion continues to operate?
accepted.x: The doctrine of severability invalidates only the inconsistent portion of a law, provided that portion can be separated from the valid remainder.
accepted.tq: Use the exact meaning of the doctrine rather than the associated case.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: The doctrine of Eclipse primarily applies to a law which is:
o: A pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
A post-Constitution law violating the rights of non-citizens only
A constitutional amendment violating the basic structure
A contractual provision waived by a citizen
accepted.x: The doctrine of eclipse mainly applies to pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights. Such laws become dormant rather than completely dead.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the scope of Eclipse and the other doctrines.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements about the doctrine of Eclipse:
1. An inconsistent pre-Constitution law becomes dormant rather than being completely wiped out.
2. The law may revive when the constitutional conflict is removed.
3. The doctrine was applied in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements are correct. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, the inconsistent law was treated as eclipsed and capable of revival after removal of the conflict through the First Amendment.
accepted.tq: Test the meaning, consequence and leading case together.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: Which case is associated with the application of the doctrine of Waiver in relation to Fundamental Rights?
o: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
Motor General Traders v. State of AP
accepted.x: In Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959), it was held that a person cannot waive a Fundamental Right.
accepted.tq: Match the doctrine with its leading case.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: With reference to the doctrine of Waiver, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: A person cannot waive a Fundamental Right, though statutory or contractual rights may be given up.
Only constitutional rights may be voluntarily given up.
Waiver applies only to rights available to non-citizens.
A citizen may permanently waive any Fundamental Right by contract.
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights cannot be waived by an individual. Statutory and contractual rights, unlike Fundamental Rights, may be relinquished.
accepted.tq: Apply the distinction between Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Doctrine)
(a) Eclipse
(b) Severability
(c) Waiver
(d) Prospective overruling

List-II (Meaning)
(i) Ruling operates only for the future
(ii) A person cannot give up a Fundamental Right
(iii) Inconsistent law remains dormant and may revive
(iv) Only the inconsistent portion of a law is void

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
accepted.x: Eclipse means dormancy and possible revival; Severability preserves the separable valid part; Waiver cannot operate against Fundamental Rights; Prospective overruling operates only in the future.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Severability — State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills
accepted.x: State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills is associated with the extension of the doctrine of Eclipse to post-Constitution laws affecting non-citizens. Severability is associated with cases such as A.K. Gopalan, R.M.D.C. and Motor General Traders.
accepted.tq: Find the wrongly assigned case rather than recalling the doctrine alone.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: The decision in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills is significant because it:
o: Introduced the doctrine of prospective overruling
Applied Eclipse to a post-Constitution law in relation to non-citizens
Established that a person may waive Fundamental Rights
Held that Fundamental Rights can never be amended
accepted.x: Ambica Mills (1974) extended the doctrine of Eclipse to post-Constitution laws operating against non-citizens.
accepted.tq: Use the distinctive qualification attached to a famous case.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: The doctrine of Progressive Interpretation treats the Constitution as:
o: A rigid document confined to the original understanding of its framers
A document subordinate to ordinary legislation
A document applicable only to disputes involving citizens
A living document to be read in accordance with present needs
accepted.x: Progressive Interpretation reads the Constitution as a living document capable of responding to present social and constitutional needs.
accepted.tq: Identify the central idea of the doctrine from its constitutional application.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: Which case is associated with the widening of Article 21 through progressive interpretation?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
accepted.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened the interpretation of Article 21 and is an important example of progressive constitutional interpretation.
accepted.tq: Link the interpretive doctrine with its constitutional example.
accepted.sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

accepted.s: Payment of wages below the minimum wage to labourers, in the circumstances recognised by the Supreme Court, amounts to:
o: A restriction on freedom of association under Article 19(4)
accepted.x: Payment below the minimum wage may amount to forced labour under Article 23, as recognised in the PUDR/Asiad case of 1982.
accepted.tq: Translate a factual situation into the applicable Fundamental Right.
accepted.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

accepted.s: A person employing a child below fourteen years in a factory or mine would violate:
accepted.x: Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment.
accepted.tq: Separate the child-exploitation provision from forced labour and discrimination provisions.
accepted.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

accepted.s: Denial of admission to a State-aided educational institution solely on the ground of religion, race, caste or language is prohibited by:
accepted.x: Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution on these grounds.
accepted.tq: Identify the specific clause governing admission to State-aided institutions.
accepted.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Excluding Dalits from a public well may violate Article 15(2).
2. Excluding Dalits from a public shop may violate Article 17.
3. The protections under Articles 15(2) and 17 may operate against private persons in such situations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Exclusion of Dalits from public facilities can attract Articles 15(2) and 17, and these protections are not confined to State action in such cases.
accepted.tq: Combine the prohibited conduct, constitutional provisions and horizontal application.
accepted.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

accepted.s: A prohibition imposed on an association can be treated as a restriction under Article 19(4) only when it is based on:
o: The grounds constitutionally permitted under Article 19(4)
Any reason considered desirable by the executive
An ordinance that is immune from judicial review
accepted.x: Restrictions on freedom of association under Article 19(4) must be based on the constitutionally specified grounds and remain subject to constitutional scrutiny.
accepted.tq: Ask whether the restriction fits the constitutional grounds rather than accepting executive discretion.
accepted.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

accepted.s: A violation of Articles 19 or 21 by a purely private individual ordinarily gives rise to:
o: An ordinary legal remedy rather than a writ remedy against the private individual
A remedy exclusively before the Election Commission
An automatic writ petition under Article 32 against that individual
accepted.x: Where the alleged violation is by a private individual and does not involve enforceable public-law action, the ordinary legal remedy is generally available rather than a writ.
accepted.tq: Distinguish enforceable public-law rights from an ordinary private-law remedy.
accepted.sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

accepted.s: Under Article 13(1), laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution which are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are:
o: Void only to the extent of inconsistency
Valid even to the extent of inconsistency
Void in their entirety in every case
accepted.x: Article 13(1) renders a pre-Constitution law void only to the extent that it conflicts with Fundamental Rights. It does not refer to laws existing before Independence as such.
accepted.tq: Watch the precise constitutional time reference and the words ‘to the extent’.
accepted.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

accepted.s: Which of the following is included within the expression ‘law’ under Article 13(3)?
o: Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage
Only a constitutional amendment made under Article 368
Only a judicial decision of the Supreme Court
Only an Act passed by Parliament
accepted.x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
accepted.tq: Test the complete statutory list rather than one familiar item.
accepted.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

accepted.s: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making a law which:
o: Changes the distribution of legislative powers only
Regulates contractual rights between private parties alone
Creates a new district within a State
Abridges or takes away the rights conferred by Part III
accepted.x: Article 13(2) declares that the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III; such a law is void to that extent.
accepted.tq: Match the constitutional clause with the prohibited legislative action.
accepted.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

accepted.s: Which constitutional amendment inserted Article 13(4), excluding constitutional amendments made under Article 368 from the operation of Article 13?
accepted.x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment Act, 1971 inserted Article 13(4), providing that Article 13 would not apply to constitutional amendments made under Article 368.
accepted.tq: Pair the specific clause with the correct amendment year.
accepted.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding constitutional amendments and Article 13:
1. In Shankari Prasad, the Supreme Court held that Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights.
2. In Golaknath, Fundamental Rights were given a transcendental position and Parliament was held unable to abridge them.
3. Kesavananda Bharati held that Fundamental Rights could be amended subject to the basic structure limitation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All three statements correctly describe the holdings associated with Shankari Prasad, Golaknath and Kesavananda Bharati.
accepted.tq: Track the constitutional position across successive landmark decisions.
accepted.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

accepted.s: Which one of the following best describes the constitutional significance of Article 13?
o: It prevents courts from examining delegated legislation.
It applies only to laws enacted before the Constitution.
It makes Fundamental Rights subordinate to ordinary legislation.
It provides the basis for judicial review and gives Fundamental Rights precedence over ordinary law.
accepted.x: Article 13 is the constitutional basis of judicial review of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights and establishes the supremacy of Fundamental Rights over ordinary law.
accepted.tq: Choose the option capturing both the function and effect of Article 13.
accepted.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

accepted.s:
Arrange the following decisions and amendments in chronological order:
A. Kesavananda Bharati case
B. Shankari Prasad case
C. Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment
D. Golaknath case
accepted.x: The correct order is Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967), Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
accepted.tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the middle developments.
accepted.sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

accepted.s: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described which constitutional provision as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution?
accepted.x: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the heart and soul of the Constitution because it provides the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
accepted.tq: Associate the famous description with the exact Article, not merely with Part III generally.
accepted.sec: Descriptions of Fundamental Rights - who said
